subtopic_detail: Timing of propranolol for a segmental facial haemangioma still in proliferative phase
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric dermatology clinic. A 7-week-old girl is brought in by her mother, who says a faint pink patch on the left cheek noticed in the first fortnight has become a raised red lesion that is enlarging weekly.

She was born at 34 weeks and weighed 1900 g. Her mother says the lesion bleeds slightly when rubbed against a bunny rug but is not painful and the baby feeds and sleeps normally.

On examination there is a bright red plaque measuring 45 mm across the left cheek, extending to the lateral upper lip and the left lower eyelid margin. The lid lesion does not currently obstruct the visual axis. There is no ulceration. There is a second 6 mm red papule on the left shoulder. Cardiovascular examination is normal and there is no lumbosacral lesion. A recent ophthalmology review documented normal fundi and no astigmatism.

data_table.Examination: Bright red plaque 45 mm across the left cheek extending to the lateral upper lip and left lower eyelid margin, visual axis clear, no ulceration, second 6 mm papule on the left shoulder
data_table.Investigations: Ophthalmology review: normal fundi, no astigmatism; cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral propranolol with dose escalation and monitoring under specialist supervision
options.rationale: A large segmental facial lesion involving the eyelid margin and lip that is still proliferating at 7 weeks carries a high risk of functional and cosmetic complication, and systemic propranolol is first-line treatment. The proliferative phase runs to roughly 5 months, so starting now captures the window in which treatment alters the trajectory rather than merely accelerating involution. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Observe with serial photographs and review in 3 months, expecting spontaneous involution
options.rationale: Most small truncal lesions can be observed safely, but a periocular and perioral segmental lesion can cause deprivation amblyopia and permanent lip distortion before involution begins. Observation would be correct for the 6 mm shoulder papule, which threatens no structure. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Start topical timolol maleate gel applied twice daily and review the lesion in 3 months
options.rationale: Topical beta blockade has useful effect only on thin superficial lesions of limited size and would not control a 45 mm segmental plaque. Timolol would be correct for the small flat shoulder papule or a superficial lesion under about 10 mm. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment of the cheek lesion and review the lesion in 3 months
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser penetrates only the superficial dermis and is used mainly for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulcerated lesions. It would be correct once the lesion has involuted and left surface vessels, not as proliferative-phase control. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile haemangioma)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone with a weaning schedule and monitoring under specialist supervision
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid was the former first-line agent but propranolol is more effective and better tolerated, so steroid is now reserved for propranolol failure or contraindication. Prednisolone would be correct where beta blockade is contraindicated, such as in significant reactive airways disease. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas follow a predictable course: a herald patch in the first weeks, rapid proliferation to about 5 months, then slow involution over years. Because the natural history is benign for most lesions, the clinical skill lies in recognising the minority that need treatment, which are those threatening vision, the airway, feeding or permanent disfigurement, and those that ulcerate. Periocular lesions can induce astigmatism and deprivation amblyopia even without covering the pupil, so ophthalmology review is part of the assessment rather than a substitute for treatment. A large segmental facial lesion also raises the question of PHACE association, which warrants cerebrovascular and cardiac imaging before beta blockade lowers perfusion pressure. Timing matters more here than in most paediatric dermatology, because a lesion allowed to complete proliferation leaves fibrofatty residue that no drug reverses.
key_points: Proliferation runs to roughly 5 months, so treatment decisions cannot wait for a routine review interval
Treat lesions threatening vision, airway, feeding, or causing ulceration or permanent disfigurement
Oral propranolol is first-line; corticosteroid is now second-line for failure or contraindication
Topical timolol is limited to thin superficial lesions of small size
Large segmental facial lesions raise the possibility of PHACE association warranting imaging
explanation.pearls: A periocular haemangioma can cause amblyopia through astigmatism from lid pressure without ever covering the pupil, so a clear visual axis does not make observation safe.

subtopic_detail: Management of a limping toddler with a normal radiograph and a low-energy twisting mechanism
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. An 18-month-old boy is brought in by his mother because he has refused to bear weight on his right leg since the previous afternoon.

His mother says he was running on a trampoline with an older cousin and caught his foot in the netting, twisting as he fell forward. He cried briefly and then went back to playing, but would not stand on the leg the next morning.

He is afebrile and systemically well. On examination he crawls readily and holds the right leg still when placed upright. Hip and knee movements are full and painless. There is minimal soft tissue swelling over the distal third of the right shin and he cries consistently on gentle torsion of the tibia. Inflammatory markers are normal. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right tibia and fibula are reported as showing no fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, crawls readily, full painless hip and knee movement, minimal swelling over distal third of right shin, pain on gentle tibial torsion
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), white cell count 9.1 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); anteroposterior and lateral tibia and fibula radiographs reported as no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and reassurance and arrange general practitioner review in 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: A normal radiograph does not exclude this fracture, and leaving an unstable tibia unsupported causes ongoing pain and refusal to weight bear. Discharge without immobilisation would be correct if tibial torsion were painless and the refusal to weight bear were unexplained by a focal sign. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Apply an above-knee cast or backslab and arrange orthopaedic review in 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: A low-energy twisting injury in a newly walking toddler with focal distal tibial tenderness and a normal radiograph is an undisplaced spiral tibial fracture, which is radiographically occult in a substantial proportion of cases at presentation. Immobilisation on clinical grounds is the standard approach, with review when periosteal reaction makes the fracture visible. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler's fracture)

options.text: Request an urgent ultrasound of the right hip to look for a joint effusion before immobilising
options.rationale: Hip movements are full and painless and the tenderness is over the distal tibia, so the hip is not the source and an effusion is not expected. Hip ultrasound would be correct for a limping child with restricted or painful hip rotation where septic arthritis or transient synovitis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Request a technetium bone scan of both lower limbs and arrange orthopaedic review in 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Bone scanning delivers a significant radiation dose and is reserved for a limping child with no localising sign after clinical and radiographic assessment. It would be correct where the site of pathology genuinely cannot be localised, which is not the case with focal tibial torsional pain. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the right tibia
options.rationale: Osteomyelitis is the important alternative but requires fever or elevated inflammatory markers, both of which are normal here, and a clear traumatic mechanism argues against it. Antibiotics and magnetic resonance imaging would be correct if the child were febrile with a raised C-reactive protein and no convincing injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: The toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft produced by a low-energy twisting force in a child in the first years of independent walking, and its defining feature is that the initial radiograph is often normal. The periosteum is thick and intact in this age group, so the fracture is stable and the injury is far less dramatic than the refusal to weight bear suggests. The diagnostic task is really one of exclusion: a normal hip examination, normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever separate it from septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, which are the diagnoses that cannot be missed. Treating on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for radiographic proof is the accepted approach, and a repeat film at 10 to 14 days shows periosteal new bone that confirms it retrospectively. Healing is reliable and long-term sequelae are rare.
key_points: Low-energy twisting in a child aged roughly 9 months to 3 years is the characteristic mechanism
Initial radiographs are frequently normal because the fracture is undisplaced and spiral
Focal pain on gentle tibial torsion localises the injury and separates it from hip pathology
Normal inflammatory markers and absence of fever argue against osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
Immobilise on clinical suspicion; periosteal reaction confirms the diagnosis on later imaging
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone appears on repeat radiographs at about 10 to 14 days, so a film taken at the 1 to 2 week orthopaedic review confirms the fracture that the presentation film missed.

subtopic_detail: First-line antiseizure choice for childhood absence epilepsy in a girl of childbearing potential
stem:
You are the resident in a paediatric neurology clinic. A 7-year-old girl is brought in by her father after her teacher reported that she blanks out in class up to 20 times a day, each time for a few seconds, and then carries on mid-sentence.

Her father has noticed the same at home and says she does not fall or shake, and there is no confusion afterwards. Development and school performance were previously normal, though her reading has slipped this term.

In clinic she is asked to blow on a paper windmill for 3 minutes. Twice she stops blowing, stares, and her eyelids flutter, then she resumes without any awareness of the pause. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. An electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background, with no photoparoxysmal response and no polyspike bursts. She has never had a myoclonic jerk or a generalised convulsion.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal; hyperventilation for 3 minutes provoked two episodes of behavioural arrest with eyelid flutter and no postictal confusion
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram: generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background, no photoparoxysmal response, no polyspike bursts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Sodium valproate, titrated to response with monitoring for weight gain and tremor
options.rationale: Valproate controls absence seizures effectively but carries dose-related teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harm, so it is avoided in females of childbearing potential when an equally effective alternative exists. It would be the choice if generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexisted, since ethosuximide does not protect against them. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Lamotrigine, titrated slowly to response with monitoring for rash and hypersensitivity
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is less effective than either ethosuximide or valproate for absence seizures and its mandatory slow titration delays control in a child having 20 events daily. It would be reasonable as third-line therapy or where both first-line agents have failed or are not tolerated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ethosuximide, titrated to response with monitoring for gastrointestinal upset
options.rationale: In typical childhood absence epilepsy without generalised convulsions, ethosuximide gives seizure freedom rates equal to valproate with significantly less attentional impairment, which matters directly given the reported decline in reading. It is preferred over valproate in a girl because it avoids the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks that accompany long-term valproate exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Carbamazepine, titrated to response with monitoring for rash and hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Sodium channel blockers aggravate generalised absence and myoclonic seizures and can precipitate absence status, so carbamazepine is contraindicated here. It would be appropriate for focal epilepsy, where the discharge is localised rather than generalised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Levetiracetam, titrated to response with monitoring for irritability and behavioural change
options.rationale: Levetiracetam has weaker evidence in absence epilepsy than the established first-line agents and was inferior in comparative trials. It is widely used in other generalised epilepsies and would be considered where first-line options have failed or behavioural monitoring is acceptable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between 4 and 10 years and is confirmed by the combination of brief behavioural arrest without postictal confusion, ready provocation by hyperventilation, and generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background. The clinical trap is that frequent brief absences are often mistaken for inattention or daydreaming, and a slipping school performance is commonly the presenting complaint rather than the seizures themselves. The comparative trial evidence is unusually clear for a paediatric epilepsy: ethosuximide and valproate control seizures equally, but valproate impairs attention more, and ethosuximide therefore wins on the outcome that matters to a child in the classroom. The important caveat is that ethosuximide has no efficacy against generalised tonic-clonic seizures, so a history of any convulsion changes the choice. Prognosis is good, with most children entering remission by adolescence.
key_points: Hyperventilation for 3 minutes provokes an absence in most untreated children and is a bedside diagnostic test
Generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background is the electroencephalographic signature
Ethosuximide and valproate are equally effective, but ethosuximide preserves attention better
Ethosuximide does not protect against generalised tonic-clonic seizures
Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine aggravate generalised absence seizures
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about any lifetime generalised convulsion before choosing ethosuximide: it has no efficacy against tonic-clonic seizures, and their presence moves the choice to valproate or lamotrigine despite the attentional and teratogenic trade-offs.

sources.label: Epilepsy Action Australia: Childhood absence epilepsy

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic and wound decision for a facial dog bite presenting outside the primary closure window
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 5-year-old girl is brought in 14 hours after the family dog bit her cheek when she leaned over its food bowl.

Her mother washed the wound with soap and water at home and did not seek care overnight because the child settled and slept. The dog is fully vaccinated, lives at home and has never left Australia.

Her immunisations are documented as up to date including four doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine. On examination there are two puncture wounds and a 20 mm curved laceration over the right cheek, 15 mm below the lower eyelid. The wound edges are moderately swollen with surrounding erythema extending 10 mm, and there is a small amount of serous discharge. She is afebrile, eating normally, and there is no facial nerve weakness and no bony step.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Two puncture wounds and a 20 mm curved cheek laceration 15 mm below the right lower eyelid, moderate oedema with 10 mm surrounding erythema and serous discharge, no facial nerve weakness, no bony step
data_table.Immunisation: Four doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis containing vaccine documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral amoxicillin with clavulanate, with immediate primary suture closure in the department
options.rationale: Primary closure of a bite presenting at 14 hours with established local inflammation traps inoculated organisms and raises the risk of deep infection. Primary closure would be correct for a clean facial bite irrigated and closed within roughly 8 hours with no signs of inflammation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral cefalexin monotherapy, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Cefalexin has unreliable activity against Pasteurella multocida and no anaerobic cover, so it is not adequate for a bite wound despite being a standard skin infection agent. It would be appropriate for uncomplicated non-bite cellulitis caused by streptococci and staphylococci. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Copious irrigation and a tetanus immunoglobulin injection, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is reserved for tetanus-prone wounds in people who are incompletely immunised or whose status is unknown, and this child has four documented vaccine doses. Immunoglobulin would be correct if fewer than three doses were documented or the history were unavailable. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Copious irrigation and oral amoxicillin with clavulanate, with plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanate covers Pasteurella multocida and the oral anaerobes that make dog bites infect, and prophylaxis is indicated for facial bites regardless of appearance. Beyond about 8 hours with established oedema and erythema the wound is left open for delayed closure or revision rather than sutured primarily. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Copious irrigation and rabies immunoglobulin with vaccine, and plastic surgery review for delayed closure
options.rationale: Australia is free of classical rabies and the only local lyssavirus reservoir is bats, so a domestic dog with no overseas travel poses no lyssavirus risk. Post-exposure prophylaxis would be correct after a bat bite or scratch in Australia, or a dog bite acquired overseas. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: Dog bites deliver a mixed inoculum of aerobes and anaerobes deep into tissue, and the two management decisions that matter are which antibiotic and whether to close. Amoxicillin with clavulanate is the Australian agent of choice because it is the only widely used oral option covering Pasteurella multocida alongside staphylococci, streptococci and anaerobes. Facial bites occupy a special position: the cosmetic stakes push toward early closure and the excellent facial blood supply makes it safer than elsewhere, but that latitude closes once the wound is several hours old and inflamed. Australia's rabies-free status means lyssavirus prophylaxis turns on bat contact or overseas acquisition rather than on the bite itself, which is a frequent source of unnecessary anxiety. Bites near the eyelid margin, over joints, or involving the hand warrant a lower threshold for specialist involvement.
key_points: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is first-line because it covers Pasteurella multocida plus anaerobes
Prophylaxis is indicated for bites to the face, hands, feet, over joints, and in immunocompromised children
Primary closure is limited to early, clean, well-irrigated wounds; inflamed or late wounds are left open
Australian domestic dogs pose no classical rabies risk; bats are the local lyssavirus reservoir
Tetanus immunoglobulin is for incomplete or unknown immunisation, not for every bite
explanation.pearls: In penicillin-allergic children the Australian bite alternative is trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole plus metronidazole, because cefalexin and clindamycin each leave Pasteurella multocida uncovered.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a markedly raised creatine kinase found during investigation of speech delay in a boy
stem:
You are the resident in a general paediatric clinic. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his mother because he is difficult to understand and is not keeping up with his kindergarten group.

His mother says he walked at 19 months, struggles with stairs and asks to be carried after short walks. He has never lost a skill he had acquired. There is no family history of neuromuscular disease.

On examination he rises from the floor by turning prone and pushing his hands up his thighs. His calves are firm and bulky. Power is 4/5 at the hip girdle and 5/5 distally, reflexes are present and symmetrical and plantar responses are flexor. There is no ptosis, no facial weakness and no fasciculation. Blood taken to investigate the developmental concern shows alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (<40), bilirubin 8 micromol/L (<20) and creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60-300).

data_table.Examination: Gowers manoeuvre positive, calf hypertrophy, proximal power 4/5 with distal power 5/5, reflexes present and symmetrical, plantar responses flexor, no ptosis or facial weakness
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 180 U/L (<40), bilirubin 8 micromol/L (<20), creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request liver ultrasound and a viral hepatitis screen and refer to a paediatric hepatology service
options.rationale: The raised aminotransferases originate from muscle rather than liver, which the normal bilirubin and grossly elevated creatine kinase indicate, so a hepatic workup pursues an artefact. Hepatology referral would be correct if gamma-glutamyl transferase were also raised and creatine kinase were normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer to a paediatric neurodisability service
options.rationale: Central imaging does not explain a creatine kinase of this magnitude, which is a muscle-specific finding, and reflexes and plantar responses are normal. Brain imaging would be correct for global delay with upper motor neuron signs, microcephaly or regression. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)

options.text: Request an open muscle biopsy for dystrophin immunostaining and refer to a neuromuscular service
options.rationale: Biopsy is invasive and is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative but clinical suspicion persists. It would be correct after deletion, duplication and sequence analysis all return negative in a boy with this phenotype. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Request nerve conduction studies with electromyography and refer to a neuromuscular service
options.rationale: Electrophysiology confirms a myopathic pattern but does not identify the cause and adds a distressing procedure when a blood test gives the diagnosis. It would be useful where a neuropathy or a neuromuscular junction disorder is suspected and creatine kinase is normal or only mildly raised. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

options.text: Request dystrophin gene deletion and duplication analysis and refer to a neuromuscular service
options.rationale: Proximal weakness with a Gowers manoeuvre, calf hypertrophy and a creatine kinase in the thousands in a boy of this age is dystrophinopathy until proven otherwise, and genetic testing has replaced muscle biopsy as the first-line confirmatory test. Deletion and duplication analysis detects around 70 per cent of causative variants, with sequencing for the remainder. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is frequently diagnosed late because the earliest presentation is developmental rather than obviously neuromuscular, with speech delay and difficulty keeping up being common first complaints. A creatine kinase discovered incidentally is often the moment the diagnosis becomes apparent, and the characteristic value is in the thousands to tens of thousands rather than the modest elevation seen with exercise or trauma. Raised aminotransferases are a well-recognised trap, because alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are both released from damaged muscle and boys are not uncommonly investigated for liver disease before anyone measures a creatine kinase. Early molecular diagnosis matters because corticosteroid therapy started before substantial function is lost prolongs ambulation, and because exon-skipping therapies depend on knowing the precise variant. Genetic confirmation also enables carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the mother and wider family.
key_points: Speech and global developmental delay are common presenting complaints before weakness is recognised
Gowers manoeuvre plus calf hypertrophy plus creatine kinase in the thousands is the diagnostic triad
Raised alanine and aspartate aminotransferase come from muscle; a normal bilirubin points away from liver
Deletion and duplication analysis is first-line and detects roughly 70 per cent of variants
Muscle biopsy is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is uninformative
explanation.pearls: Measure creatine kinase in any boy with unexplained developmental delay who is not yet walking by 18 months or who has isolated aminotransferase elevation with a normal bilirubin and gamma-glutamyl transferase.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
